description: We’re doing the storytelling challenge. There’s a lot of NASA hardware still sitting on the Moon and Mars — rovers, landers, bits of old missions — and most people don’t know what any of it did. We want to dig into the mission data and photos and tell the story behind a few of these objects in a way that’s actually fun to read.
summary:
What happens when a space mission ends? 

The discoveries remain, but the stories behind them are often forgotten. Since the 1960s, NASA has sent countless rovers, landers, and probes across our solar system. Yet once their missions conclude, these remarkable machines are often reduced to archived reports and technical documents buried in dense websites, making their stories difficult for younger audiences to discover.

Lost Rovers aims to change that.

 Created in response to NASA’s “Abandoned but Not Forgotten” challenge, Lost Rovers is an interactive, pixel-art storytelling website built around real NASA mission data. Visitors become newly recruited NASA Explorers and receive a briefing from mission director Dr. Rosalind Grace before travelling across five worlds. There, they meet the Apollo 15 ALSEP station on the Moon, Sojourner on Mars, Galileo at Jupiter, Huygens on Titan, and Voyager 2 beyond Neptune.

Each machine tells its own story, introducing visitors to its mission, the technology behind it, and the discoveries it made. This brings these often-forgotten pieces of space history to life, making them more than paragraphs in a textbook. 

With interactive chapters, collectible tokens, music, narration, and animation, Lost Rovers transforms learning into an immersive journey, allowing young audiences to discover the history of space exploration at their own pace.

Because a mission ending shouldn’t mean a story ending.
details:
Project Overview & How It Works

What it does:

Lost Rovers is a collection of interactive, retro-style stories that teach young audiences about equipment left behind in space and the scientific advances it made possible. The equipment is personified and narrates its own journey, creating a deeper connection with visitors. Interactive and musical elements engage young space enthusiasts, making them feel as though they are experiencing each story firsthand.

How it works:

The explorer (the user) learns that rovers and other pieces of space equipment are gradually being forgotten. After meeting Dr. Rosalind Grace, who sends them on a mission to explore NASA’s past expeditions, the explorer chooses where in space to go. At each destination, abandoned equipment narrates its own story. The experience also includes interactive elements that visitors can use by clicking or dragging. After completing a story, the explorer receives a Polaroid token featuring a detail from their journey.

Benefits & Intended Impact

Key benefits:

The project teaches the history of space exploration through visuals and interactive storytelling. By presenting the equipment as characters, it creates an emotional connection with young audiences and makes the information fun and accessible.

Intended impact:

Through these interactive stories, we hope to make the history of space exploration more accessible to young enthusiasts and spark their curiosity, encouraging them to keep learning about the subject’s past and future.

Software, Coding Languages and Tools Used:

Coding languages: HTML, CSS, and JavaScript

Software and tools:

• Procreate, Canva, and Creatify for designing backgrounds and animation elements

• Netlify for hosting

• Web Audio API (originally synthesized soundtrack - no audio files)

Music Inspiration: C418’s Minecraft soundtracks inspired the mood of each world. All music in the project is original.

Creativity & Design Considerations

What makes it creative:

The project combines retro-style animation with tactile interactive elements. Each story is written from the equipment’s point of view, adding an emotional layer and giving each story its own soundtrack and atmosphere. Sound effects accompany each action. We also created a token for each story, giving visitors a memorable detail to take away.

Factors considered:

We designed the experience to make navigation between destinations and the main mission-control area easy. We separated important events to make the information easier to understand. Although the animations are pixelated, we kept the text clear and readable. We also tailored each piece of equipment’s dialogue and tone to its individual persona, since each was left behind under different circumstances.
